title: The Levite and the Crime at Gibeah

date.label: Undated Judges narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Judges 19 depicts the sexual assault of an unnamed concubine at Gibeah
claims.evidence: Judges 19:22–26 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). The men of Gibeah surround the host's house and demand the guest be brought out; the host pleads and offers his virgin daughter and the concubine; the Levite thrusts his concubine outside to them, they assault her through the night, and in the morning she collapses at the doorway of the house, her hands on the threshold. The text does not explicitly narrate the exact moment of her death. Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

claims.claim: Tell el-Ful is an important proposed location of Gibeah; the identification is contested, and archaeology does not establish the assault in Judges 19 or the battles in Judges 20.
claims.evidence: Gibeah archaeological overview, Gibeah of Saul / Tell el-Ful, Biblical Archaeology website, read in full (92 lines): the setting of Gibeah is often linked to Tell el-Ful, but the identification remains contested and no excavated evidence substantiates the specific assault, the Levite's journey, or the ensuing battles. William F. Albright, excavation report on Tell el-Ful (1924): the case rests on topography rather than on any object found in the ground — Tell el-Ful stands on the main watershed route about six kilometres north of Jerusalem and three kilometres south of Ramah; Albright concluded that "no topographical point in Palestine is more certainly fixed than the identity of Tell el-Ful with Gibeah of Benjamin and Saul," citing Josephus's account of Titus's march and Jerome's account of Paula's pilgrimage; he dated the earliest remains to Iron I, with a village founded about 1230 BCE and a fortress about 1200 BCE. Cynthia Edenburg, Dismembering the Whole: Composition and Purpose of Judges 19–21 (2016), peer-reviewed monograph: the phases of the fortress were determined by supposing changes in its architecture, their dating depended on the biblical traditions about Gibeah, and even the surviving corner cannot be properly dated since its stratigraphy is unclear; Amihai Mazar pointed out that the paucity of Iron I and early Iron II finds does not accord with the biblical descriptions of Gibeah as an established city; Israel Finkelstein (2011) proposed the structure is a tower typical of Assyrian military and administrative construction, built in the Iron IIC period, and rejected the identification with Gibeah of Saul; Edenburg's summary is that Gibeah was sparsely populated until the eighth century and the depiction of Gibeah in Judges 19–20 as a premonarchic urban community has no basis in the archaeological record. (JCL-11-002's registry source_ids is S020;S029; S020 has no registry entry and does not enter sources[] — see review.notes; the claim is grounded by S029, Albright1924, and Edenburg.) The identification stays contested, with both sides stated and neither presented as settled; archaeology does not establish the assault in Judges 19 or the battles in Judges 20.

claims.claim: Genesis 19 and Judges 19 share recognizable guest-threat narrative patterns
claims.evidence: Judges 19:22–25 and Genesis 19:4–8 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). In both passages travelers arrive, hospitality is offered, a crowd threatens the guests, and the household becomes the scene of danger; the outcomes differ — in Genesis 19 the threatened guests are rescued, the attackers are blinded, and the city is destroyed by divine judgement, while in Judges 19 no rescue comes: the concubine is thrust outside, assaulted through the night, and dies at the threshold. United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, note on Judges 19:22–25: this part of the story "closely parallels that of the assault on Lot's angelic visitors in Gn 19:4–8." Literary pattern only; the recognition of the pattern does not by itself settle the date or direction of literary dependence. Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

connections.note: Shared hospitality-threat structure; distinct locations and characters (Genesis 19:1–11). This is a literary/thematic relation, not an independently verified shared historical event.
Explicit prophetic reference to days of Gibeah (Hosea 9:9). This is a literary/thematic relation, not an independently verified shared historical event.
